steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: Start with the very small CUP/RING at an individual spikelet's base, and a DENSE HAIR RING for the true leaf ligule. Texas cupgrass is a robust perennial rooted BUNCH (not a rhizomatous sodgrass) with soft leaves and short closely pressed flowering racemes holding silky spikelets. The existing photo shows visible spikelets and axis but NOT the tiny cup or leaf collar: inspect a macro before confirming.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: 1. BUNCH: new gallery panel 5 shows ACTUAL source-identified in-ground leafy tuft among dry litter with upright green culms. Roots are not exposed, nor is a same-root entire flowering plant independently traceable. Do not arrow underground anatomy.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: E. sericea — tufted perennial commonly about 0.3–1.2 m; soft blades, ring of straight ligular hairs, small fuzzy clustered spikelets on short hair-bearing stalks; tiny cup at spikelet base. Paspalum spp. — can have spikelets in one-sided racemes but lack the diagnostic Eriochloa cup-like lower attachment; their ligule is generally membranous rather than a dense hair ring. Digitaria spp. — often spreading grasses with fingerlike racemes and paired spikelets; no Eriochloa cup at each spikelet base. Inspect the same-plant base and spikelet attachments. Panicum spp. — open or contracted panicles, but do not share the cup-like spikelet base; check spikelet, stalk, ligule with magnification.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: DRY HEAD — real archived narrow flowering panicle
panels.image_role: Existing physical JPEG, source-determined Eriochloa sericea; narrow dried flowering head and visible small lateral units, photographed against fingers
panels.caption: Look at the narrow axis and many tiny lateral spikelet-like units. A finger provides rough visual context, NOT a millimeter scale. The decisive cup at an individual spikelet base, glume/lemma boundaries and ligule cannot be resolved here.
panels.why_it_matters: Useful dry-stage comparison with the original greener flowering head. Do not confuse visible feathery hairs with a verified basal cup.

panels.label: TEXAS CUPGRASS — actual living tuft with narrow leafy basal shoots
panels.image_role: In-ground living grass bunch with radiating narrow blades and upright flowering culms in source-identified stand; soil conceals root origin and individual flower-to-root identity
panels.caption: Previously archived original source-labelled Texas cupgrass by Theresa Strickler. A green central tuft of long narrow basal blades and upright slender culms is photographed in natural dry leaf litter. Several flowering axes are visible within the broader photographed field, but belowground roots are not exposed. This is the source-identified plant's actual live growth form, not a dug-out specimen or independently vouchered same-root flowering culm.
panels.why_it_matters: Crew can recognize the genuine living basal bunch in dry woodland field habitat alongside its diagnostic flowering-head and basal cup photographs.
